recurring_scale_anchors: 304×192 canvas; keep television programs inside a visible broadcast frame when the medium matters.
No readable words, captions, station logos, brands, letters or numerals; use blank bars, icons and scene imagery only.
Vary program scenes instead of relying on a generic presenter or TV silhouette for every genre.
Make TV equipment, program content and viewing actions distinct through camera, remote, antenna, cable, satellite, screen and viewer cues.
Keep faces, remote buttons and screen scenes large enough to read at card size; avoid graphic crime and unsafe imagery.

polysemy_resolution_table.breakfast tv: A morning television program with presenters, a bright sunrise studio, and a breakfast table; not a cooking demonstration.
polysemy_resolution_table.cartoon: An animated television show with a clearly drawn character inside a TV screen; follow the broadcast-program sense.
polysemy_resolution_table.chat show: A studio program in which a host chats with one guest on a sofa before a small audience.
polysemy_resolution_table.children’s show: A television program made for children, with a friendly puppet or playful presenter on screen.
polysemy_resolution_table.children’s tv: Television content for young viewers, shown through a child watching bright, age-appropriate programs.
polysemy_resolution_table.comedy: A funny scripted television scene with a harmless visual gag; keep it distinct from a multi-character sitcom.
polysemy_resolution_table.cooking show: A television chef demonstrates food preparation at a kitchen counter directly to a camera.
polysemy_resolution_table.costume drama: A scripted TV story whose ornate historical costumes are the defining cue; not a modern drama in fancy clothes.
polysemy_resolution_table.crime: A fictional crime-program genre showing an investigator studying clues; no real victim or graphic crime.
polysemy_resolution_table.current affairs: A TV panel discussing a topical public issue with a chart or news image; deeper discussion than a brief bulletin.
polysemy_resolution_table.documentary: A nonfiction TV program showing a real-world subject being observed or interviewed, without fictional staging.
polysemy_resolution_table.drama: A serious scripted television story with actors in an emotional conflict inside a TV frame.
polysemy_resolution_table.game show: A television contest with a host, contestant and physical game mechanism such as a wheel; not a question quiz.
polysemy_resolution_table.nature documentary: A wildlife subject filmed in its natural habitat with a visible documentary camera or long lens.
polysemy_resolution_table.news: A television news bulletin with a presenter and a broadcast monitor; the program, not the anchor’s job.
polysemy_resolution_table.period drama: A scripted TV story set in a clearly historical place, with architecture and period clothing; not a modern story with costumes alone.
polysemy_resolution_table.quiz show: A TV host asks contestants a knowledge question and they reach for buzzers; no written words or numerals.
polysemy_resolution_table.reality tv: Unscripted participants are followed by a visible camera during an everyday challenge; not actors on a scripted set.
polysemy_resolution_table.satire: A television comedian or caricature mocks a pompous fictional authority figure; use visual exaggeration, not written jokes.
polysemy_resolution_table.sitcom: A recurring comedy about a familiar group in a home or workplace set, with several characters and a light comic mishap.
polysemy_resolution_table.soap opera: An ongoing emotional TV serial about relationships, shown through expressive characters in a domestic scene; no literal soap.
polysemy_resolution_table.sports program: A studio sports commentator analyzes game action on a replay monitor; distinct from a live sports broadcast.
polysemy_resolution_table.sports show: A televised sports broadcast with a presenter, field action and camera coverage; distinct from the broader sports category.
polysemy_resolution_table.talk show: A presenter leads a studio conversation with several guests at a desk or panel; broader and more structured than a sofa chat.
polysemy_resolution_table.thriller: A suspenseful fictional TV scene with a character noticing a looming threat; keep it non-supernatural and non-graphic.
polysemy_resolution_table.tv program: One general television program shown on a TV screen with broadcast cues, without choosing a specific genre.
polysemy_resolution_table.show / shows: Television shows as a varied group of programs, represented by several different program images on screens.
polysemy_resolution_table.sports: Sports as televised content, with a clear game in progress and broadcast camera coverage.
polysemy_resolution_table.cable tv: A home television service connected to a coaxial cable and wall outlet; no satellite dish.
polysemy_resolution_table.channel: A selected television channel indicated by a remote changing the program on screen; not a waterway.
polysemy_resolution_table.music channel: A TV channel broadcasting a live musician or music video with abstract musical symbols, without logos.
polysemy_resolution_table.remote: A handheld television remote control pointed toward a TV; make its buttons and infrared cue clear.
polysemy_resolution_table.satellite tv: A television receiver getting a signal from a satellite dish and a satellite above; not cable television.
polysemy_resolution_table.screen: The flat electronic display surface of a television, not a theater projection surface or window mesh.
polysemy_resolution_table.shopping channel: A TV host demonstrates a product on screen while a viewer watches; keep the shopping broadcast context clear.
polysemy_resolution_table.tv: Television as a viewing medium in a home, with moving program content and a broadcast signal.
polysemy_resolution_table.tv set: The physical television receiver with screen, bezel and stand; distinguish the appliance from the programs it carries.
polysemy_resolution_table.video on demand: A viewer selects one program from on-screen choices and starts it when they want; not a live schedule.
polysemy_resolution_table.streaming: A TV video program arriving over a wireless internet connection on a screen; not music-only streaming or a river.
polysemy_resolution_table.volume: The sound level of a TV, shown by a speaker and rising or falling sound bars; not the volume of a book.
polysemy_resolution_table.adverts: A sequence of TV advertising spots presenting different consumer products; no written product labels.
polysemy_resolution_table.commercial break: A TV show is interrupted by an inserted advertisement, shown as a break between program scenes.
polysemy_resolution_table.episode: One installment of an ongoing television series, singled out from related installments.
polysemy_resolution_table.preview: A short teaser for a program that will be shown later, displayed on a TV before the main program.
polysemy_resolution_table.series: Several linked episodes featuring recurring characters, shown as a continuing TV series rather than one episode.
polysemy_resolution_table.subtitles: Two blank caption bars along the lower edge of a television picture; no letters or numbers.
polysemy_resolution_table.tv guide: A printed booklet with a grid of TV programs and times, not a transit timetable.
polysemy_resolution_table.tv schedule: A time-ordered television lineup with repeated program blocks and clock symbols; distinct from a printed guide booklet.
polysemy_resolution_table.commercial: One television advertisement showing a product demonstration in a broadcast frame; not the break between programs.
polysemy_resolution_table.season / seasons: A grouped run of episodes from one TV series, represented by multiple related program cards; not weather seasons.
polysemy_resolution_table.couch potato: A habitual TV watcher slumped on a couch with a remote and snacks; the person is inactive, not a literal potato.
polysemy_resolution_table.host: A TV show host welcomes guests and keeps the program moving; not a hotel host or communion wafer.
polysemy_resolution_table.interview: A television presenter asks a guest questions in a studio while a camera records them; not a hiring interview.
polysemy_resolution_table.news anchor: A lead news presenter at a broadcast desk facing the camera, with a world-news monitor behind them.
polysemy_resolution_table.newsreader: A presenter reading from a paper bulletin at a studio desk; distinguish the reading action from a lead anchor.
polysemy_resolution_table.presenter: A TV presenter introduces a segment beside a monitor; no guest interview or news desk is needed.
polysemy_resolution_table.reporter: A journalist reports from an outdoor location with a handheld microphone and a camera operator.
polysemy_resolution_table.catch-up tv: A viewer chooses a previously missed episode from a TV service and watches it later; show a replay cue.
polysemy_resolution_table.change channel: A hand presses a channel button on a remote as the television picture changes to a different program.
polysemy_resolution_table.record: A TV program is captured by a recorder or DVR while it is being broadcast; show the TV and recording device.
polysemy_resolution_table.turn off: A viewer presses a TV power control and the previously lit screen goes dark.
polysemy_resolution_table.turn on: A viewer presses a TV power control and the previously dark screen lights up with a program.
polysemy_resolution_table.turn up the volume: A hand presses the volume-up control as TV sound waves grow stronger; no text or digits.

glossary_context_notes: The chapter group resolves broad glosses toward television: channel is a broadcast channel, remote is a remote control, volume is sound level, host is a presenter, record is capturing a TV program, and season is a series season.

Distinguish close neighbors: children’s show vs children’s TV, chat show vs talk show, game show vs quiz show, crime vs documentary, current affairs vs news, news anchor vs newsreader vs reporter, sports program vs sports show, program vs series vs episode vs season, and adverts vs commercial vs commercial break.
Use the TV receiver for appliance terms; use a TV frame for broadcast-program genres; use a camera or network cue for filming and streaming actions.
